 By Pete Sampson Nov. 12, 2026 Updated 2:40 pm EST Share article Wake Forest has agreed to a contract extension with Jake Dickert, keeping the 43-year-old head coach in Winston-Salem for the foreseeable future, the school announced . Wake Forest described the deal as “long-term” but did not release details of the extension.
 In two seasons leading the Demon Deacons, Dickert has built Wake Forest into one of the Atlantic Coast Conference’s upper-echelon programs. After a 9-4 debut season following Dickert’s move from Washington State, the program is now positioned to challenge for a College Football Playoff berth, 8-1 on the year and ranked 13th with a lone loss to Miami. Wake Forest closes the regular season with games at SMU and Georgia Tech before hosting Duke.
 CFP inclusion or not, Wake Forest has hit double-digit wins just twice in school history.
 Advertisement
 “Wake Forest University is committed to football success at the highest level and Coach Dickert has done an extraordinary job of inspiring belief among our players, fans and the entire Demon Deacon community,” Wake Forest athletic director John Currie said in a statement. “I am grateful for his and Candice’s commitment and trust and especially appreciate President Rodriguez and our Board leadership recognizing that now was the time to go ahead and eliminate any outside speculation so that our team and Deacon Nation can put all our energy into the stretch run of this special season.”
 Dickert would have been an attractive candidate in the upcoming coaching carousel, considering his ability to manage transitions while winning with less. The Wisconsin native landed his first head coaching job after Washington State fired Nick Rolovich in October 2021, then guided the Cougars to a 23-20 record over the next 3 1/2 seasons despite the Cougars’ place among the power conferences crumbling with the demise of the Pac-12 in its traditional form.
 When Dickert made the cross-country move to Wake Forest, he was tasked with replacing Dave Clawson, whose 11-year run included an ACC title but produced poor results at the end of his tenure; the Demon Deacons finished near the bottom of the conference in his final two seasons.
 Dickert’s profile has risen to the point that his commentary on the utility of conferences in the 24-team CFP world gained traction earlier this week. That’s not standard practice for the head coach of a program that usually lives on the fringe of the sport’s consciousness.
 “To not say we’re going to have conference champions, why do we have conferences?” Dickert said. “I know there’s a lot of things that go into all that. Just feels odd.”
 With Dickert signed to a contract extension, Wake Forest is betting on its coach to keep the program in the national discourse for seasons to come.
